listen_text: Section. Introduction. Induction is an important proof technique which is used, in different forms, in almost all areas of logic, theoretical computer science, and mathematics. It is needed to prove many of the results in logic. Induction is often contrasted with deduction, and characterized as the inference from the particular to the general. For instance, if we observe many green emeralds, and nothing that we would call an emerald that's not green, we might conclude that all emeralds are green. This is an inductive inference, in that it proceeds from many particular cases (this emerald is green, that emerald is green, etc.) to a general claim (all emeralds are green). Mathematical induction is also an inference that concludes a general claim, but it is of a very different kind than this “simple induction.” Very roughly, an inductive proof in mathematics concludes that all mathematical objects of a certain sort have a certain property. In the simplest case, the mathematical objects an inductive proof is concerned with are natural numbers. In that case an inductive proof is used to establish that all natural numbers have some property, and it does this by showing that List. Next item. zero has the property, and Next item. whenever a number k has the property, so does k plus one . End list. Induction on natural numbers can then also often be used to prove general claims about mathematical objects that can be assigned numbers. For instance, finite sets each have a finite number n of elements, and if we can use induction to show that every number n has the property “all finite sets of size n are and so on ” then we will have shown something about all finite sets. Induction can also be generalized to mathematical objects that are inductively defined. For instance, expressions of a formal language such as those of first-order logic are defined inductively. Structural induction is a way to prove results about all such expressions. Structural induction, in particular, is very useful—and widely used—in logic. End section.

listen_text: Section. Induction on the natural numbers . In its simplest form, induction is a technique used to prove results for all natural numbers. It uses the fact that by starting from zero and repeatedly adding one we eventually reach every natural number. So to prove that something is true for every number, we can (one) establish that it is true for zero and (two) show that whenever it is true for a number n , it is also true for the next number n plus one . If we abbreviate “number n has property capital P ” by capital P of n (and “number k has property capital P ” by capital P of k , etc.), then a proof by induction that capital P of n for all n is a natural number consists of: List. Next item. a proof of capital P of zero , and Next item. a proof that, for any k , if capital P of k then capital P of k plus one . End list. To make this crystal clear, suppose we have both (one) and (two). Then (one) tells us that capital P of zero is true. If we also have (two), we know in particular that if capital P of zero then capital P of zero plus one , that is, capital P of one . This follows from the general statement “for any k , if capital P of k then capital P of k plus one ” by putting zero for k . So by modus ponens, we have that capital P of one . From (two) again, now taking one for n , we have: if capital P of one then capital P of two . Since we've just established capital P of one , by modus ponens, we have capital P of two . And so on. For any number n , after doing this n times, we eventually arrive at capital P of n . So (one) and (two) together establish capital P of n for any n is a natural number . Source anomaly note. listen_text: Section. Strong Induction. In the principle of induction discussed above, we prove capital P of zero and also if capital P of k , then capital P of k plus one . In the second part, we assume that capital P of k is true and use this assumption to prove capital P of k plus one . Equivalently, of course, we could assume capital P of k minus one and use it to prove capital P of k —the important part is that we be able to carry out the inference from any number to its successor; that we can prove the claim in question for any number under the assumption it holds for its predecessor. There is a variant of the principle of induction in which we don't just assume that the claim holds for the predecessor k minus one of k , but for all numbers smaller than k , and use this assumption to establish the claim for k . This also gives us the claim capital P of n for all n is a natural number . For once we have established capital P of zero , we have thereby established that capital P holds for all numbers less than one . And if we know that if capital P of l for all l is less than k , then capital P of k , we know this in particular for k equals one . So we can conclude capital P of one . With this we have proved capital P of zero and capital P of one , that is, capital P of l for all l is less than two , and since we have also the conditional, if capital P of l for all l is less than two , then capital P of two , we can conclude capital P of two , and so on. In fact, if we can establish the general conditional “for all k , if capital P of l for all l is less than k , then capital P of k ,” we do not have to establish capital P of zero anymore, since it follows from it. For remember that a general claim like “for all l is less than k , capital P of l ” is true if there are no l is less than k . This is a case of vacuous quantification: “all capital A s are capital B s” is true if there are no capital A s, for every x, if capital A of x, then capital B of x is true if no x satisfies capital A of x . In this case, the formalized version would be “ for every l, if l is less than k, then capital P of l ”—and that is true if there are no l is less than k . And if k equals zero that's exactly the case: no l is less than zero , hence “for all l is less than zero , capital P of zero ” is true, whatever capital P is. A proof of “if capital P of l for all l is less than k , then capital P of k ” thus automatically establishes capital P of zero . Source anomaly note. Source wording note. listen_text: Section. Inductive Definitions. In logic we very often define kinds of objects inductively, that is, by specifying rules for what counts as an object of the kind to be defined which explain how to get new objects of that kind from old objects of that kind. For instance, we often define special kinds of sequences of symbols, such as the terms and formulas of a language, by induction. For a simple example, consider strings consisting of letters the letter a , the letter b , the letter c , the letter d , the symbol the circle operator , and brackets an opening square bracket and a closing square bracket , such as “ the malformed string opening bracket, opening bracket, c circle d, closing bracket, opening bracket ”, “ the malformed string opening bracket, a, opening bracket, closing bracket, circle, closing bracket ”, “ the letter a ” or “ the bracketed term whose left component is the bracketed term a circle b and whose right component is d ”. You probably feel that there's something “wrong” with the first two strings: the brackets don't “balance” at all in the first, and you might feel that the “ the circle operator ” should “connect” expressions that themselves make sense. The third and fourth string look better: for every “ an opening square bracket ” there's a closing “ a closing square bracket ” (if there are any at all), and for any the circle operator we can find “nice” expressions on either side, surrounded by a pair of parentheses. We would like to precisely specify what counts as a “nice term.” First of all, every letter by itself is nice. Anything that's not just a letter by itself should be of the form “ the bracketed term t circle s ” where s and t are themselves nice. Conversely, if t and s are nice, then we can form a new nice term by putting a the circle operator between them and surround them by a pair of brackets. We might use these operations to define the set of nice terms. This is an inductive definition. Definition. Nice terms. The set of nice terms is inductively defined as follows: List. Next item. Any letter the letter a , the letter b , the letter c , the letter d is a nice term. Next item. If s sub one and s sub two are nice terms, then so is the bracketed term s sub one circle s sub two . Next item. Nothing else is a nice term. End list. End definition. This definition tells us that something counts as a nice term if and only if it can be constructed according to the two conditions (one) and (two) in some finite number of steps. In the first step, we construct all nice terms just consisting of letters by themselves, that is, Displayed expression. the letters a, b, c, and d. End displayed expression. In the second step, we apply (two) to the terms we've constructed. We'll get Displayed expression. the bracketed terms a circle a, a circle b, b circle a, and so on through d circle d. End displayed expression. for all combinations of two letters. In the third step, we apply (two) again, to any two nice terms we've constructed so far. We get new nice term such as the bracketed term whose left component is a and whose right component is the bracketed term a circle a —where t is the letter a from step one and s is the bracketed term a circle a from step two—and the bracketed term whose left component is the bracketed term b circle c and whose right component is the bracketed term d circle b constructed out of the two terms the bracketed term b circle c and the bracketed term d circle b from step two. And so on. Clause (three) rules out that anything not constructed in this way sneaks into the set of nice terms. Note that we have not yet proved that every sequence of symbols that “feels” nice is nice according to this definition. However, it should be clear that everything we can construct does in fact “feel nice”: brackets are balanced, and the circle operator connects parts that are themselves nice. The key feature of inductive definitions is that if you want to prove something about all nice terms, the definition tells you which cases you must consider. For instance, if you are told that t is a nice term, the inductive definition tells you what t can look like: t can be a letter, or it can be the bracketed term s sub one circle s sub two for some pair of nice terms s sub one and s sub two . Because of clause (three), those are the only possibilities. When proving claims about all of an inductively defined set, the strong form of induction becomes particularly important. For instance, suppose we want to prove that for every nice term of length n , the number of an opening square bracket in it is is less than n divided by two . This can be seen as a claim about all n : for every n , the number of an opening square bracket in any nice term of length n is is less than n divided by two . Proposition. For any n , the number of an opening square bracket in a nice term of length n is is less than n divided by two . End proposition. Proof. To prove this result by (strong) induction, we have to show that the following conditional claim is true: Quotation. If for every l is less than k , any nice term of length l has is less than l divided by two an opening square bracket apostrophe s , then any nice term of length k has is less than k divided by two an opening square bracket apostrophe s . End quotation. To show this conditional, assume that its antecedent is true, that is, assume that for any l is less than k , nice terms of length l contain is less than l divided by two an opening square bracket apostrophe s . We call this assumption the inductive hypothesis. We want to show the same is true for nice terms of length k . So suppose t is a nice term of length k . Because nice terms are inductively defined, we have two cases: (one) t is a letter by itself, or (two) t is the bracketed term s sub one circle s sub two for some nice terms s sub one and s sub two . text: Section. Inductive Definitions. In logic we very often define kinds of objects inductively, that is, by specifying rules for what counts as an object of the kind to be defined which explain how to get new objects of that kind from old objects of that kind. For instance, we often define special kinds of sequences of symbols, such as the terms and formulas of a language, by induction. For a simple example, consider strings consisting of letters the letter a , the letter b , the letter c , the letter d , the symbol the circle operator , and brackets an opening square bracket and a closing square bracket , such as “ the malformed string opening bracket, opening bracket, c circle d, closing bracket, opening bracket ”, “ the malformed string opening bracket, a, opening bracket, closing bracket, circle, closing bracket ”, “ the letter a ” or “ the bracketed term whose left component is the bracketed term a circle b and whose right component is d ”. You probably feel that there's something “wrong” with the first two strings: the brackets don't “balance” at all in the first, and you might feel that the “ the circle operator ” should “connect” expressions that themselves make sense. The third and fourth string look better: for every “ an opening square bracket ” there's a closing “ a closing square bracket ” (if there are any at all), and for any the circle operator we can find “nice” expressions on either side, surrounded by a pair of parentheses. We would like to precisely specify what counts as a “nice term.” First of all, every letter by itself is nice. Anything that's not just a letter by itself should be of the form “ the bracketed term t circle s ” where s and t are themselves nice. Conversely, if t and s are nice, then we can form a new nice term by putting a the circle operator between them and surround them by a pair of brackets. We might use these operations to define the set of nice terms. This is an inductive definition. Definition. Nice terms. The set of nice terms is inductively defined as follows: List. Next item. Any letter the letter a , the letter b , the letter c , the letter d is a nice term. Next item. If s sub one and s sub two are nice terms, then so is the bracketed term s sub one circle s sub two . Next item. Nothing else is a nice term. End list. End definition. This definition tells us that something counts as a nice term if and only if it can be constructed according to the two conditions (one) and (two) in some finite number of steps. In the first step, we construct all nice terms just consisting of letters by themselves, that is, Displayed expression. the letters a, b, c, and d. End displayed expression. In the second step, we apply (two) to the terms we've constructed. We'll get Displayed expression. the bracketed terms a circle a, a circle b, b circle a, and so on through d circle d. End displayed expression. for all combinations of two letters. In the third step, we apply (two) again, to any two nice terms we've constructed so far. We get new nice term such as the bracketed term whose left component is a and whose right component is the bracketed term a circle a —where t is the letter a from step one and s is the bracketed term a circle a from step two—and the bracketed term whose left component is the bracketed term b circle c and whose right component is the bracketed term d circle b constructed out of the two terms the bracketed term b circle c and the bracketed term d circle b from step two. And so on. Clause (three) rules out that anything not constructed in this way sneaks into the set of nice terms. Note that we have not yet proved that every sequence of symbols that “feels” nice is nice according to this definition. However, it should be clear that everything we can construct does in fact “feel nice”: brackets are balanced, and the circle operator connects parts that are themselves nice. For instance, if you are told that t is a nice term, the inductive definition tells you what t can look like: t can be a letter, or it can be the bracketed term s sub one circle s sub two for some pair of nice terms s sub one and s sub two . This can be seen as a claim about all n : for every n , the number of an opening square bracket in any nice term of length n is is less than n divided by two . Proposition. For any n , the number of an opening square bracket in a nice term of length n is is less than n divided by two . End proposition. Proof. When we have defined a set of objects (such as the natural numbers or the nice terms) inductively, we can also define relations on these objects by induction. For instance, consider the following idea: a nice term t sub one is a subterm of a nice term t sub two if it occurs as a part of it. Let's use a symbol for it: t sub one is a subterm of t sub two . Every nice term is a subterm of itself, of course: t is a subterm of t . We can give an inductive definition of this relation as follows: Definition. The relation of a nice term t sub one being a subterm of t sub two , t sub one is a subterm of t sub two , is defined by induction on t sub two as follows: List. Next item. If t sub two is a letter, then t sub one is a subterm of t sub two if and only if t sub one equals t sub two . Next item. If t sub two is the bracketed term s sub one circle s sub two , then t sub one is a subterm of t sub two if and only if t sub one equals t sub two , t sub one is a subterm of s sub one , or t sub one is a subterm of s sub two . End list. End definition. This definition, for instance, will tell us that the letter a is a subterm of the bracketed term b circle a . For (two) says that the letter a is a subterm of the bracketed term b circle a if and only if the letter a equals the bracketed term b circle a , or the letter a is a subterm of b , or the letter a is a subterm of the letter a . The first two are false: the letter a clearly isn't identical to the bracketed term b circle a , and by (one), the letter a is a subterm of the letter b if and only if the letter a equals the letter b , which is also false. However, also by (one), the letter a is a subterm of the letter a if and only if the letter a equals the letter a , which is true. text: Section. Relations and Functions. When we have defined a set of objects (such as the natural numbers or the nice terms) inductively, we can also define relations on these objects by induction. For instance, consider the following idea: a nice term t sub one is a subterm of a nice term t sub two if it occurs as a part of it. Let's use a symbol for it: t sub one is a subterm of t sub two . Every nice term is a subterm of itself, of course: t is a subterm of t . We can give an inductive definition of this relation as follows: Definition. The relation of a nice term t sub one being a subterm of t sub two , t sub one is a subterm of t sub two , is defined by induction on t sub two as follows: List. Next item. If t sub two is a letter, then t sub one is a subterm of t sub two if and only if t sub one equals t sub two . Next item. If t sub two is the bracketed term s sub one circle s sub two , then t sub one is a subterm of t sub two if and only if t sub one equals t sub two , t sub one is a subterm of s sub one , or t sub one is a subterm of s sub two . End list. End definition. This definition, for instance, will tell us that the letter a is a subterm of the bracketed term b circle a . For (two) says that the letter a is a subterm of the bracketed term b circle a if and only if the letter a equals the bracketed term b circle a , or the letter a is a subterm of b , or the letter a is a subterm of the letter a . The first two are false: the letter a clearly isn't identical to the bracketed term b circle a , and by (one), the letter a is a subterm of the letter b if and only if the letter a equals the letter b , which is also false. However, also by (one), the letter a is a subterm of the letter a if and only if the letter a equals the letter a , which is true. It's important to note that the success of this definition depends on a fact that we haven't proved yet: every nice term t is either a letter by itself, or there are uniquely determined nice terms s sub one and s sub two such that t equals the bracketed term s sub one circle s sub two . “Uniquely determined” here means that if t equals the bracketed term s sub one circle s sub two it isn't also equals the bracketed term r sub one circle r sub two with s sub one is not equal to r sub one or s sub two is not equal to r sub two . If this were the case, then clause (two) may come in conflict with itself: reading t sub two as the bracketed term s sub one circle s sub two we might get t sub one is a subterm of t sub two , but if we read t sub two as the bracketed term r sub one circle r sub two we might get not t sub one is a subterm of t sub two . Before we prove that this can't happen, let's look at an example where it can happen. Definition. Define bracketless terms inductively by List. Next item. Every letter is a bracketless term. Next item. If s sub one and s sub two are bracketless terms, then s sub one circle s sub two is a bracketless term. Next item. Nothing else is a bracketless term. End list. End definition. Bracketless terms are, for example, the letter a , the string b circle d , the string b circle a circle b . Now if we defined “subterm” for bracketless terms the way we did above, the second clause would read If t sub two equals s sub one circle s sub two , then t sub one is a subterm of t sub two if and only if t sub one equals t sub two , t sub one is a subterm of s sub one , or t sub one is a subterm of s sub two . Now the string b circle a circle b is of the form s sub one circle s sub two with Displayed expression. first decomposition: s sub one equals the letter b, and s sub two equals a circle b; it is also of the form r sub one circle r sub two, where r sub one equals b circle a and r sub two equals b. End displayed expression. Now is the letter a circle the letter b a subterm of the string b circle a circle b ? The answer is yes if we go by the first reading, and no if we go by the second. The property that the way a nice term is built up from other nice terms is unique is called unique readability. Since inductive definitions of relations for such inductively defined objects are important, we have to prove that it holds. Proposition. Suppose t is a nice term. Then either t is a letter by itself, or there are uniquely determined nice terms s sub one , s sub two such that t equals the bracketed term s sub one circle s sub two . End proposition. Proof. If t is a letter by itself, the condition is satisfied. So assume t isn't a letter by itself. We can tell from the inductive definition that then t must be of the form the bracketed term s sub one circle s sub two for some nice terms s sub one and s sub two . It remains to show that these are uniquely determined, that is, if t equals the bracketed term r sub one circle r sub two , then s sub one equals r sub one and s sub two equals r sub two . So suppose t equals the bracketed term s sub one circle s sub two and also t equals the bracketed term r sub one circle r sub two for nice terms s sub one , s sub two , r sub one , r sub two . We have to show that s sub one equals r sub one and s sub two equals r sub two . First, s sub one and r sub one must be identical, for otherwise one is a proper initial segment of the other. But by the proposition on proper initial segments of nice terms , that is impossible if s sub one and r sub one are both nice terms. But if s sub one equals r sub one , then clearly also s sub two equals r sub two . End proof. We can also define functions inductively: for example, we can define the function f that maps any nice term to the maximum depth of nested an opening square bracket, an ellipsis, and a closing square bracket in it as follows: Definition. The depth of a nice term, f of t , is defined inductively as follows: Displayed expression. f of t is defined by cases: zero if t is a letter; and the maximum of f of s sub one and f of s sub two, plus one, if t is the bracketed term s sub one circle s sub two; end cases. End displayed expression. End definition. For instance Displayed expression. f of the bracketed term a circle b equals the maximum of f of a and f of b, plus one, which equals the maximum of zero and zero plus one, which equals one; and f of the bracketed term whose left component is the bracketed term a circle b and whose right component is c equals the maximum of f of the bracketed term a circle b and f of c, plus one, which equals the maximum of one and zero plus one, which equals two. End displayed expression. Here, of course, we assume that s sub one an s sub two are nice terms, and make use of the fact that every nice term is either a letter or of the form the bracketed term s sub one circle s sub two . It is again important that it can be of this form in only one way. To see why, consider again the bracketless terms we defined earlier. The corresponding “definition” would be: Displayed expression. g of t is defined by cases: zero if t is a letter; and the maximum of g of s sub one and g of s sub two, plus one, if t equals s sub one circle s sub two; end cases. End displayed expression. Now consider the bracketless term the string a circle b circle c circle d . End displayed expression.
